subject: physics

items.q: Which statement about a standing wave on a string is correct?
items.correct: It forms where two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose.
items.misconception: It is a single wave that has stopped travelling, so its crests stay in fixed places.
items.why: The names "standing" and "stationary" wave suggest a wave that has come to a halt, and standing-wave diagrams show a fixed pattern of loops with no arrows, so nothing in the picture shows the two travelling waves that produce it. Think of the incident wave and its reflection passing through each other. At every point their displacements add, so the pattern of nodes and antinodes stays fixed while both waves keep moving. A crest does not stay in one place: each antinode moves from a crest to a trough and back every cycle.
items.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
items.random_wrong: It carries energy along the string from the source towards the far end.

items.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its first harmonic. At one instant every point on the string has zero displacement, so the string is straight. Which statement about the string at this instant is correct?
items.correct: Points between the ends are moving at their greatest speeds; its energy is all kinetic.
items.misconception: Every point is momentarily at rest; its energy is all stored as elastic potential energy.
items.why: Students mix up displacement and velocity, a confusion well documented for simple harmonic motion: a point at the centre of its motion "is not anywhere", so it seems not to be moving. In everyday use, being at a position and being still sound alike. Treat each point on the string as a simple harmonic oscillator. Its speed is greatest as it passes through the equilibrium position and zero at its maximum displacement. When the whole string is straight, every point except the nodes is moving at its greatest speed.
items.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
items.random_wrong: The two waves have cancelled each other out, so the string holds no energy at this instant.

items.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave. Its nodes are at x = 0, 0.40 m, 0.80 m and 1.20 m, measured from one end. Points P, Q and R on the string are at x = 0.10 m, 0.20 m and 0.70 m. Which statement about the oscillations of P, Q and R is correct?
items.correct: P and R oscillate in antiphase, with equal amplitudes.
items.misconception: P and Q oscillate π/4 rad out of phase, being λ/8 apart.
items.why: Students first learn phase difference for travelling waves, where Δφ = 2πx/λ is correct, and apply the same rule to standing waves without noticing that the two situations differ. In a standing wave every point between two adjacent nodes reaches its maximum displacement at the same instant. Across a node the direction of displacement reverses, so the phase jumps by π. Two points λ/8 apart in the same section are in phase, not π/4 rad apart.
items.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
items.random_wrong: P and Q oscillate in phase, with amplitudes equal to each other.

items.q: A vibrator of frequency 320 Hz sets up a standing wave on a stretched string. The distance between adjacent nodes is 0.45 m. What is the speed of the travelling waves on the string?
items.correct: 288 m s⁻¹
items.misconception: 144 m s⁻¹
items.why:
A standing-wave diagram draws each loop with an upper and a lower curve, which looks like a crest and a trough together, and a crest plus a trough is one wavelength of a travelling wave. Taking the length of a string in its first harmonic as one wavelength is a common error in written answers. The upper and lower curves of a loop show the same section of string at two different instants, half a period apart; they are not a crest followed by a trough. The string at any one instant has only one half-wave in each loop, so the node-to-node distance is λ/2 and a string in its first harmonic holds half a wavelength.

Working: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 2 × 0.45 m = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 Hz × 0.90 m = 288 m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
items.random_wrong: 576 m s⁻¹
items.working: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart: λ = 2 × 0.45 m = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 Hz × 0.90 m = 288 m s⁻¹.

items.q: A pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Where along the pipe is the displacement of the air zero at all times?
items.correct: At the closed end of the pipe
items.misconception: Midway between the two ends
items.why: Students picture sound as air being pushed against the closed end, so they expect the most vigorous vibration there. The closed end is also where the sound reflects, which sounds like the most active part of the pipe. Displacement means the movement of the air along the pipe. The solid end stops the air next to it from moving at all, so the displacement there is zero at all times: a node. The air has its largest displacement at an open end.
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.random_wrong: At both ends of the pipe

items.q: A string of length 0.80 m is fixed at both ends. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the third harmonic?
items.correct: 450 Hz
items.misconception: 300 Hz
items.why:
Students count features on a diagram to identify the harmonic and choose nodes, the most visible points, without checking the count on the first harmonic, which has two nodes but is harmonic number 1. Check with the first harmonic: two nodes (the fixed ends), one loop, one antinode. The harmonic number matches the number of loops (or antinodes), so the third harmonic has three loops, three antinodes and four nodes.

Working: Two fixed ends: λ_n = 2L/n. λ₃ = 2 × 0.80 m/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240 m s⁻¹/0.533 m = 450 Hz. (Check: f₁ = v/2L = 240/1.60 = 150 Hz, and f₃ = 3f₁ = 450 Hz.)
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.random_wrong: 900 Hz
items.working: Two fixed ends: λ_n = 2L/n. λ₃ = 2 × 0.80 m/3 = 0.533 m. f₃ = v/λ₃ = 240 m s⁻¹/0.533 m = 450 Hz. (Check: f₁ = v/2L = 240/1.60 = 150 Hz, and f₃ = 3f₁ = 450 Hz.)

items.q: A string of length 0.60 m is fixed at one end. Its other end is free: it is tied to a light ring that slides without friction on a vertical rod. The speed of waves on the string is 240 m s⁻¹. Which gives the harmonic number n, the wavelength λ and the frequency f of the standing wave with the next frequency above that of the first harmonic?
items.why:
The string fixed at both ends, with all harmonics, is the first and most familiar case, and "harmonic series" is learned as 1, 2, 3, … before other boundary conditions are met. Apply the boundary conditions. With a node at one end and an antinode at the other, the length must hold an odd number of quarter-wavelengths: L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, … so f = f₁, 3f₁, 5f₁, … A pattern at 2f₁ would need the same kind of boundary at both ends.

Working: One fixed end (node) and one free end (antinode): λ_n = 4L/n with n odd. First harmonic: λ₁ = 4 × 0.60 m = 2.40 m, f₁ = 240/2.40 = 100 Hz. Next mode: n = 3, λ₃ = 4 × 0.60/3 = 0.80 m, f₃ = 240/0.80 = 300 Hz.
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.working: One fixed end (node) and one free end (antinode): λ_n = 4L/n with n odd. First harmonic: λ₁ = 4 × 0.60 m = 2.40 m, f₁ = 240/2.40 = 100 Hz. Next mode: n = 3, λ₃ = 4 × 0.60/3 = 0.80 m, f₃ = 240/0.80 = 300 Hz.

items.q: A pipe of length 0.68 m is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air in the pipe is 340 m s⁻¹. Which gives, in increasing order, the lowest frequencies at which the air in the pipe resonates?
items.misconception: f = 125 Hz and no other
items.why:
Resonance is introduced with systems such as a mass on a spring or a pendulum, which have one natural frequency, and it is described as "the natural frequency" in the singular. Students carry this over to strings and pipes. The speed of waves on a given string (or of sound in the air) is fixed by the medium, so f = v/λ: a harmonic with one-third of the wavelength has three times the frequency. Each harmonic is a separate natural frequency at which the string or air column can resonate.

Working: Closed end: node; open end: antinode. λ_n = 4L/n, n odd. λ₁ = 4 × 0.68 m = 2.72 m; f₁ = 340 m s⁻¹/2.72 m = 125 Hz. f₃ = 3 × 125 = 375 Hz; f₅ = 5 × 125 = 625 Hz.
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.working: Closed end: node; open end: antinode. λ_n = 4L/n, n odd. λ₁ = 4 × 0.68 m = 2.72 m; f₁ = 340 m s⁻¹/2.72 m = 125 Hz. f₃ = 3 × 125 = 375 Hz; f₅ = 5 × 125 = 625 Hz.

items.q: A lightly damped mass–spring system has a natural frequency of 2.0 Hz. It is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude with a frequency of 3.5 Hz. Which describes its oscillation once the amplitude has become steady?
items.correct: At 3.5 Hz, with a smaller amplitude than when driven at 2.0 Hz
items.misconception: At 2.0 Hz, its natural frequency, with a small steady amplitude
items.why:
Students learn that every system has a natural frequency at which it "likes" to oscillate, and they meet this frequency first in free oscillations, so they expect it to appear whatever is done to the system. Distinguish free and forced oscillations. Free: the system oscillates at its natural frequency. Forced: in the steady state it oscillates at the driving frequency, and the amplitude is large only when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency.

Working: Steady forced oscillation is at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. Driving at 2.0 Hz equals the natural frequency (resonance), so the amplitude at 3.5 Hz is smaller than at 2.0 Hz.
items.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
items.random_wrong: At 3.5 Hz, with a larger amplitude than when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
items.working: Steady forced oscillation is at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. Driving at 2.0 Hz equals the natural frequency (resonance), so the amplitude at 3.5 Hz is smaller than at 2.0 Hz.

items.q: A singer shatters a wine glass by singing one steady note close to it. Which condition is essential for this to happen?
items.correct: The note's frequency is equal to a natural frequency of the glass.
items.misconception: The note is very loud, whatever frequency the singer chooses.
items.why: In everyday experience a bigger push gives a bigger movement, so students look for the size of the force, not its timing. Pushing a child on a swing is described as "pushing harder" rather than "pushing at the right moment". For a given force, the amplitude of a driven oscillator depends strongly on the driving frequency. A child on a swing goes high because small pushes are given at the swing's natural frequency, so each push adds energy; the same pushes at the wrong frequency would sometimes oppose the motion.
items.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
items.random_wrong: The note is the highest frequency that the singer is able to produce.

items.q: A radio receiver contains a circuit whose natural frequency can be adjusted. Signals from many stations, each broadcasting at a different frequency, reach its aerial at the same time. How does the receiver pick out one station?
items.correct: Its natural frequency is set equal to that station's frequency, so it resonates with it.
items.misconception: It responds most strongly to the signal with the highest frequency reaching it.
items.why: More pushes per second sounds like more energy supplied, and in everyday experience shaking something faster makes it move more. The idea of matching a frequency is less intuitive than "more is more". Above the natural frequency the driving force is increasingly out of step with the motion, so for much of each cycle it acts against the motion and the energy transferred per cycle falls. The amplitude peaks near the natural frequency and falls on either side.
items.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
items.random_wrong: It responds most strongly to the strongest signal, whatever its frequency.

items.q: A lightly damped oscillator is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude, and its steady amplitude is measured over a range of driving frequencies. The damping is then increased slightly, and the measurements are repeated. Which describes the new response curve compared with the first?
items.correct: The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly lower frequency.
items.misconception: The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly higher frequency.
items.why: Students associate resistance with stiffness, and a stiffer spring does raise the natural frequency. Sketched response curves for heavier damping are often drawn with the peak moved to the right. Damping is a resistive force that opposes the velocity; it does not act like a stiffer spring. More damping makes the system respond more sluggishly, so the frequency of maximum amplitude moves slightly lower, and the peak becomes lower and broader.
items.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
items.random_wrong: The maximum amplitude is unchanged, and it occurs at the same frequency.

items.q: The same oscillator is driven by a periodic force of the same constant amplitude in two experiments, X and Y, with different damping. In X the maximum amplitude is 25 mm, at 5.00 Hz, and the amplitude falls to half this value at 4.82 Hz and 5.17 Hz. In Y the maximum amplitude is 3.4 mm, at 4.89 Hz, and the amplitude falls to half this value at 3.3 Hz and 6.1 Hz. Which conclusion do the data support?
items.correct: Y is more heavily damped: its peak is lower, wider and at a slightly lower frequency.
items.misconception: Only X shows resonance; Y's damping is too heavy for resonance to occur.
items.why: Resonance is often introduced with dramatic examples, such as shattered glasses and collapsing structures, and defined as "the amplitude becomes very large", so students think of it as all-or-nothing. Resonance is the maximum in the frequency response near the natural frequency. Damping lowers and widens that maximum but, while the damping is light, does not remove it. The amplitude is finite because energy is dissipated as fast as it is supplied.
items.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
items.random_wrong: X is more heavily damped, because its peak is at the higher frequency.

items.q: A mass–spring system is displaced from equilibrium and released. Which statement about the effect of damping on its motion is correct?
items.correct: Heavy damping: no oscillation, but a slower return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
items.misconception: Heavy damping: no oscillation, and a quicker return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
items.why: Damping is described as "stopping the oscillation", so more of it seems to stop things faster. The words "heavy" and "critical" both suggest "a lot", so students rank them by amount of damping rather than by the time taken. Damping opposes motion in both directions: it stops the system overshooting but also slows its return. With heavy damping the system creeps back towards equilibrium. Critical damping is the balance: just enough to prevent oscillation, so the return is the fastest possible without overshoot.
items.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
items.random_wrong: Critical damping: it passes through equilibrium once, then comes to rest at equilibrium.

items.q: A door closer damps the motion of a heavy door. With the damping first set low, the door, released from wide open, swings past the closed position and back several times before settling. The damping is then increased in small steps. Which describes how the door's motion changes?
items.correct: The swinging past stops at critical damping; beyond it, the door closes more slowly.
items.misconception: At critical damping the door swings past just once, then stops at the closed position.
items.why: Critical damping is often loosely described as "stopping the oscillation within about one cycle", and students picture the quickest stop as a single swing. Critical damping is defined as the least damping for which the system does not oscillate. Any overshoot through the equilibrium position is an oscillation, however small, so a system that overshoots is lightly damped.
items.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
items.random_wrong: The swinging past stops at critical damping; beyond it, the door closes even more quickly.

items.q: A pipe is open at both ends. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Which statement about the motion of the air is correct?
items.correct: The air at the midpoint of the pipe does not oscillate.
items.misconception: The air at each open end oscillates side to side across the pipe.
items.why: Pipe diagrams draw the displacement envelope as curves across the pipe, in the same way as a vibrating string, and students read the graph as a picture of the air's motion. The curves are a graph: their height across the pipe shows how large the air's displacement is at each position along the pipe. The displacement itself is along the pipe, because sound is longitudinal.
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.random_wrong: The air at each open end of the pipe does not oscillate.

items.q: The diagram shows the envelope of a standing wave on a string of length L = 1.20 m that is fixed at both ends. What is the wavelength of the waves on the string?
items.why:
Both λ/2 and λ/4 appear in standing-wave work, and students who memorise them as isolated facts attach the wrong one to the wrong pair of points. Picture one loop: node, antinode, node. The whole loop is λ/2, so node to antinode is half of that, λ/4, and node to next node is λ/2.

Working: The envelope has three loops between the fixed ends. Each loop (node to node) is half a wavelength, so L = 3λ/2 and λ = 2L/3 = 2 × 1.20 m / 3 = 0.80 m.
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.working: The envelope has three loops between the fixed ends. Each loop (node to node) is half a wavelength, so L = 3λ/2 and λ = 2L/3 = 2 × 1.20 m / 3 = 0.80 m.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal string held between two fixed supports, one at each end, with the distance between the supports marked L = 1.20 m. The standing-wave envelope is drawn as three equal loops between the supports: a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve that touch the dashed equilibrium line at the two supports and at two equally spaced points between them, and are furthest apart at the middle of each loop.

items.q: The diagram shows the displacement envelope of the air in a pipe of length L = 0.85 m that is closed at one end and open at the other. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What is the frequency of the sound?
items.correct: 300 Hz
items.misconception: 385 Hz
items.why:
Students who remember that wave speed, frequency and wavelength are linked, but not how, sometimes divide the two given quantities instead of multiplying them; checking units (m s⁻¹ = s⁻¹ × m) would catch this. Check the units: f/λ has units s⁻¹ m⁻¹, which is not a speed. A wave advances one wavelength in each period, so v = λ/T = fλ.

Working: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode. The pattern has a node at the closed end, one more node inside the pipe and an antinode at the open end, so L = 3λ/4: λ = 4L/3 = 4 × 0.85 m / 3 = 1.13 m. f = v/λ = 340 m s⁻¹ / 1.133 m = 300 Hz (the third harmonic of the pipe).
items.specStatementText: standing waves patterns in strings and pipes
items.random_wrong: 600 Hz
items.working: The closed end is a displacement node and the open end an antinode. The pattern has a node at the closed end, one more node inside the pipe and an antinode at the open end, so L = 3λ/4: λ = 4L/3 = 4 × 0.85 m / 3 = 1.13 m. f = v/λ = 340 m s⁻¹ / 1.133 m = 300 Hz (the third harmonic of the pipe).

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal pipe drawn as a shaded rectangle with a thick wall at the left end, labelled closed end, and no wall at the right end, labelled open end; the length between the ends is marked L = 0.85 m. Inside the pipe the displacement envelope is drawn as a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve. They meet on the dashed centre line at the closed end and again at a point two thirds of the way along the pipe, and are furthest apart one third of the way along and at the open end, where the envelope ends wide open.

items.q: The diagram shows the envelope of a standing wave on a string of length L, driven by a vibrator at its left end and fixed at its right end. The amplitude of the vibrator is so small that both ends of the string can be treated as nodes. P and Q are points on the string. At one instant, P has its maximum displacement, upward. Which describes Q at that instant?
items.correct: Q is displaced downward by the same amount as P.
items.misconception: Q is displaced upward by exactly the same amount as P.
items.why: Textbooks emphasise that points between two nodes are in phase and that a standing wave has no progressive phase change, and students generalise this to the whole wave, ignoring the reversal at each node. Look at the two sections either side of a node. When one is at its maximum upward displacement, the other is at its maximum downward displacement. Points in adjacent sections are π rad out of phase; points two sections apart are in phase again.
items.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
items.random_wrong: Q is moving through its equilibrium position.

figure.alt: Diagram of a horizontal string running from a small box labelled vibrator at the left to a fixed support at the right. The standing-wave envelope has two equal loops: a solid upper curve and a dashed lower curve that meet on the dashed equilibrium line at both ends and at the midpoint of the string. A dimension line below marks the two halves of the string as L/2 and L/2. Two red dots on the equilibrium line mark points P and Q: P is a quarter of the way along the left-hand loop from the midpoint node, and Q the same distance to the right of the midpoint node in the right-hand loop.

items.q: The graph shows how the steady amplitude of a lightly damped mass–spring system depends on the frequency of the periodic force that drives it. The amplitude of the driving force is kept constant while its frequency is reduced slowly from 8.0 Hz to 2.0 Hz. Which describes the amplitude of the mass–spring system during this change?
items.correct: It rises to a maximum as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz, then falls again.
items.misconception: It falls throughout, because a slower driving force transfers less energy to the system.
items.why:
More pushes per second sounds like more energy supplied, and in everyday experience shaking something faster makes it move more. The idea of matching a frequency is less intuitive than "more is more". Above the natural frequency the driving force is increasingly out of step with the motion, so for much of each cycle it acts against the motion and the energy transferred per cycle falls. The amplitude peaks near the natural frequency and falls on either side.

Working: The peak of the response curve, read from the graph, is at about 5 Hz: this is the natural frequency of the system. Reducing the driving frequency from 8.0 Hz brings it towards 5 Hz, so the amplitude rises; it is greatest as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance) and then falls as the driving frequency continues down to 2.0 Hz.
items.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency
items.random_wrong: It stays the same throughout, because the amplitude of the driving force does not change.
items.working: The peak of the response curve, read from the graph, is at about 5 Hz: this is the natural frequency of the system. Reducing the driving frequency from 8.0 Hz brings it towards 5 Hz, so the amplitude rises; it is greatest as the driving frequency passes about 5 Hz (resonance) and then falls as the driving frequency continues down to 2.0 Hz.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis, marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10). The curve starts at a small amplitude at low frequency, rises slowly at first and then steeply to a single sharp peak close to 5 Hz, then falls steeply and flattens out towards a very small amplitude by 8 Hz and beyond.

items.q: Curve X on the graph shows how the steady amplitude of a driven oscillator varies with driving frequency. One change is then made to the apparatus, and the measurements are repeated to give curve Y. Which change was made?
items.correct: The damping acting on the oscillator was increased.
items.misconception: The amplitude of the driving force was reduced.
items.why: Damping is first taught through free oscillations dying away, so students connect it only with decay. When a driver is present, they assume it simply makes up the losses. At resonance the energy supplied per cycle by the driver equals the energy removed per cycle by damping. Greater damping removes more energy at a given amplitude, so the balance is reached at a smaller amplitude: the peak is lower.
items.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation
items.random_wrong: The damping acting on the oscillator was made smaller.

figure.alt: Graph of amplitude (vertical axis, no scale) against driving frequency / Hz (horizontal axis marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8) with two curves. Curve X, blue, has a tall narrow peak at 4 Hz and falls steeply to small amplitudes on either side. Curve Y, red, has a peak about one third as high as X's, much broader, and centred slightly below 4 Hz. At frequencies well below the peaks (under about 2 Hz) and well above them (over about 6 Hz) the two curves almost coincide.

items.q: The graph shows displacement–time curves X, Y and Z for the same mass–spring system, released from rest at the same displacement with three different amounts of damping. Which statement about the curves is correct?
items.correct: Y shows critical damping: it reaches equilibrium in the least time without crossing it.
items.misconception: X shows heavy damping: even heavy damping leaves a small oscillation before rest.
items.why: The standard "damped oscillation" graph is a sine curve with a shrinking envelope, and everyday examples (a plucked ruler, a swing, a guitar string) are all lightly damped, so students never see a damped system that does not oscillate. The behaviour depends on how much damping there is. Light damping: oscillation with decreasing amplitude. Critical damping: the quickest return without oscillation. Heavy damping: a slow return without oscillation.
items.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.
items.random_wrong: Y shows heavy damping: the heaviest damping gives the quickest return to equilibrium.

figure.alt: Graph of displacement x (vertical axis) against t / s (horizontal axis marked 0, 2, 4, 6, 8). All three curves start at the same positive displacement at t = 0. Curve X, blue, falls, crosses the time axis at about 2.8 s, dips a little below it, and then returns to the axis, on which it lies from about 6.5 s onwards. Curve Y, red, falls smoothly to the axis without crossing it and is almost on it by about 5 s. Curve Z, dashed, falls more slowly than Y, never crosses the axis, and is still clearly above it at 8 s.

items.q: Does a standing wave transfer energy along the medium?
items.correct: No. The two travelling waves carry energy at equal rates in opposite directions, so there is no net transfer of energy along the medium. The energy stays in each section between nodes.
items.misconception: A standing wave carries energy along the medium from the source to the far end, as every wave does.
items.why: The first definition of a wave that students learn is "a disturbance that transfers energy without transferring matter", and they apply it to every wave, including standing waves. A standing wave is two travelling waves carrying energy in opposite directions at equal rates, so the net transfer is zero. The nodes never move, so no work is done across them and no energy passes through them; within each section, energy changes back and forth between kinetic and elastic potential energy.
items.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When the whole string of a standing wave is momentarily straight, have the waves and their energy disappeared?
items.correct: No. The two travelling waves still exist and simply cancel in displacement at that instant. The energy is still in the string, as kinetic energy of the moving string.
items.misconception: When two waves cancel to give zero displacement everywhere, the waves, and the energy they carry, are destroyed at that instant.
items.why: Physics-education research on overlapping pulses finds that many students think two pulses that cancel have destroyed each other. Seeing a straight string suggests that nothing is there. Superposition adds displacements, not energies. When the displacements cancel, the velocities of the string do not: each point is moving at its greatest speed, so the energy is all kinetic. A moment later the string is displaced again, which could not happen if the waves had been destroyed.
items.specStatementText: the nature and formation of standing waves in terms of superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all points of a standing wave oscillate with the same amplitude?
items.correct: No. The amplitude varies with position: zero at the nodes, greatest at the antinodes, and intermediate between them.
items.misconception: Every point on a standing wave oscillates with the same amplitude, as the points on a travelling wave do.
items.why: Along a travelling wave every point does oscillate with the same amplitude, and the word "amplitude" is used for the wave as a whole. Students carry this over to standing waves. A standing wave has no single amplitude for all points. The amplitude of each point depends on its distance from the nearest node: zero at the node and greatest (2A) at the antinode, λ/4 away.
items.specStatementText: nodes and antinodes, relative amplitude and phase difference of points along a standing wave
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every end of a string or pipe a displacement node?
items.correct: No. Only a boundary where the medium cannot move is a node: a fixed end of a string, or a closed end of a pipe. A free end of a string and an open end of a pipe are displacement antinodes.
items.misconception: Every end of a vibrating string or air column is a node, as the ends of a guitar string are.
items.why: Standing waves are usually introduced with strings fixed at both ends, such as guitar and violin strings, where both ends are nodes. Students generalise "ends are nodes" to every boundary. Ask whether the medium can move at the boundary. A fixed end cannot, so it is a node. A free end of a string, or the air at an open end of a pipe, is free to move and oscillates with the greatest amplitude, so it is an antinode.

items.q: Is the harmonic above the first harmonic always called the second harmonic?
items.correct: No. A harmonic is named by the ratio of its frequency to the first-harmonic frequency. For a pipe closed at one end, the mode above the first harmonic has 3f₁, so it is the third harmonic; there is no second harmonic.
items.misconception: Harmonics are numbered in order, so the second-lowest mode of any string or pipe is the second harmonic.
items.why: In everyday counting, the item after the first is the second, and musicians number the modes of an instrument in order. Naming a harmonic by its frequency ratio rather than its position in the list is less intuitive than counting. The harmonic number n is defined by f_n = nf₁. Work out the frequency ratio first, then name the harmonic: for a closed–open system the ratios are 1, 3, 5, …, so the modes are the first, third and fifth harmonics.

items.q: Is resonance the same as an echo, sound reflecting and building up?
items.correct: No. An echo is the reflection of a sound. Resonance is a large-amplitude oscillation of a system driven at one of its natural frequencies.
items.misconception: Resonance means sound echoing or reverberating, so a sound that reflects back and forth resonates.
items.why: In everyday language "resonant" describes a hall or a voice that rings or echoes, and "resonate" is often used to mean "reverberate". Ask what is being driven and at what frequency. Resonance requires a system with a natural frequency and a periodic driving force at that frequency. Reflection alone, such as an echo from a cliff, involves no natural frequency and is not resonance.
items.specStatementText: the nature of resonance including natural frequency and amplitude of oscillation based on driving frequency

items.q: Does damping lower the whole frequency-response curve by the same factor, leaving its shape unchanged?
items.correct: No. Damping has its greatest effect near the natural frequency. It lowers and widens the peak, but far from the natural frequency the amplitude is almost unchanged.
items.misconception: Adding damping reduces the amplitude at every driving frequency by the same factor, so the damped curve is a scaled-down copy of the undamped one.
items.why: Students treat damping as a general loss that affects everything equally, like turning down a volume control, and sketches of response curves are often drawn as similar shapes of different heights. Well below the natural frequency the amplitude is set mainly by the spring and the size of the force, and well above it mainly by the mass, so damping matters little there. Near resonance, damping is what limits the amplitude, so its effect is concentrated at the peak.
items.specStatementText: the effect of damping on the maximum amplitude and resonant frequency of oscillation

items.q: Does the time period of a lightly damped oscillation change as its amplitude decreases?
items.correct: No. With light damping the time period stays almost constant while the amplitude decreases. (It is very slightly longer than the undamped period, but does not change as the oscillation dies away.)
items.misconception: As a lightly damped oscillation dies away, its time period changes: with a smaller amplitude there is less distance to travel, so each oscillation takes less time.
items.why: The belief that a smaller swing takes less time is one of the best-documented ideas about pendulums; students reason from distance alone and overlook that the speed is also smaller. With a smaller amplitude the oscillator has less distance to cover but also moves more slowly, and for simple harmonic motion the two effects cancel: the period does not depend on amplitude. Light damping reduces the amplitude cycle by cycle while the period stays almost unchanged.
items.specStatementText: the effects of light, critical and heavy damping on the system.

items.q: Do the loops of a standing wave on a string get smaller with distance from the vibrator that drives it?
items.correct: No. In a standing wave every antinode has the same amplitude, however far it is from the vibrator, because the wave and its reflection have equal amplitudes all along the string. Points at equal distances from a node have equal amplitudes wherever they are on the string.
items.misconception: The amplitude of a standing wave decreases along the string away from the vibrator, because the wave loses energy as it travels from its source.
items.why: Students carry over the picture of a travelling wave spreading out and weakening as it moves away from its source (ripples on a pond, sound fading with distance), and some draw standing waves with loops that shrink towards the far end. A standing wave is the superposition of a wave and its reflection, which have the same amplitude everywhere on a string with negligible loss. The amplitude of a point depends only on where it lies between the nodes, not on its distance from the vibrator: every antinode has the same amplitude, and two points at the same distance from a node have the same amplitude.
